text: Microsoft Entra Connect — the tool formerly called Azure AD Connect — is what actually keeps on-prem Active Directory and Entra ID consistent with each other. It's installed on a Windows Server on-prem, and it's the piece that makes the hybrid identity from Lesson 1 real instead of theoretical. Without it, the two directories would simply drift apart.

Entra Connect reads objects out of on-prem AD — users, groups, devices, contacts, with their core attributes like userPrincipalName and display name — and applies sync rules that decide what gets created or updated as a matching object in Entra ID. An administrator can scope exactly what syncs, excluding service accounts or specific organizational units. Passwords are never sent as plaintext; what moves for authentication is covered in the next lesson.

That sync runs on a scheduler, by default every 30 minutes, as a delta cycle that only picks up what's changed since the last run. The ADSync PowerShell module exposes it directly: Get-ADSyncScheduler shows the current schedule and last run time, and Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta forces an immediate delta sync — Initial forces a full re-import of everything in scope, which is also what runs automatically the very first time Entra Connect is set up.

Core sync is one-way, on-prem AD to Entra ID, every cycle. Edit a synced user's attribute directly in the Entra ID portal and the next cycle silently overwrites it, because on-prem AD is still the source of truth. Writeback is the opt-in exception: password writeback lets a self-service reset in Entra ID flow back down to on-prem AD, so the new password still works for on-prem sign-ins too.

Entra Connect gets accounts synchronized — but it doesn't decide how a sign-in is actually verified. That's Lesson 3: password hash sync versus federation, the two real ways authentication gets handled once an account exists in both directories.
